fact: On macOS a button given .keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction) (Return, no modifiers) is drawn as the default button with special coloration automatically; if several controls carry it, only the first is emphasized.
HIG: the primary (default) button uses the app accent color, responds to Return, and in a temporary view (sheet, alert, editable view) lets the view close automatically when Return is pressed.
.cancelAction is the Escape key with no modifiers. The doc says nothing about any visual treatment for it on macOS.

In confirmationDialog the default button is shown with more prominence (influenced via .defaultAction), the system may reorder buttons by role and prominence, and a .cancel-role button replaces the built-in dismiss action.
ButtonRole gained .confirm and .close (macOS 26); .confirm marks a button that confirms an operation (example: toolbar save in a sheet). How it renders on macOS is not described.
.automatic button style: on a plain canvas macOS uses the bordered style; inside a container (e.g. List) it resolves to that container's recommended style for the platform.

Buttons adapt their look automatically to List rows, context menus, Form and most other interactive containers; a role (e.g. destructive) is styled by the system per context. The exact resolved style per container (List, Form, Menu, alert, sheet) is not named.
macOS toolbar items do not include a bezel; the system supplies hover and selection appearances. Use Button(title, systemImage:) or Label so the button can adapt to toolbars and menus.
A button inside a sheet gets no special style beyond the automatic (bordered) one; any sheet-specific default style is not stated.
ControlSize.regular is the default control size; .extraLarge exists and resolves to .large outside visionOS.
Toggle .automatic on macOS is a checkbox in most contexts; in toolbar content it becomes the button style; in a Menu it shows a checkmark when on. A Form-specific default is not stated.

HIG macOS: prefer a checkbox for a single on/off setting; use a switch only for emphasized settings that govern a group; inside a grouped form consider a mini switch so row heights match; don't put switches, checkboxes or radio buttons in a toolbar.

Picker .automatic on macOS is a pop-up button in a standard view, and may change with context such as a container. Defaults for Form or toolbar are not stated. In a macOS Form, .inline gives radio buttons.
TextField .automatic is the platform- and context-recommended style; the concrete macOS appearance is not stated.

Form applies platform styling to buttons, toggles, labels etc.; on macOS the default form renders as aligned vertical stacks (iOS: grouped list). .grouped gives leading labels and trailing controls in visually grouped sections.

Toolbar label display (icon only / title and icon / title only) is a ToolbarLabelStyle set at the scene; binding it via windowToolbarLabelStyle(_:) makes it user-configurable; .automatic picks the best fit.
Toolbars take on Liquid Glass automatically and group items onto shared backgrounds; ToolbarSpacer (.fixed or flexible) separates groups, and users can add or move spacers in customizable toolbars.

HIG: avoid toolbar backgrounds and tinted controls; prefer borderless system symbols over text; keep at most about three groups; keep text-labeled items apart from symbol items; mark exactly one key action (Done/Submit) as prominent, on the trailing side.
The system adds the toolbar overflow menu automatically on macOS; don't add one by hand. Every toolbar item must also exist as a menu bar command.
On macOS 15+, List and Form get the seamless window/titlebar background by default; scrollContentBackground(.hidden) turns it off, and making it visible makes a ScrollView seamless.

Sidebars float in the Liquid Glass layer (more opaque for legibility). On macOS, row height, text and glyph size follow the user's sidebar icon size setting. Sidebar icons use the accent color by default.

In the Liquid Glass release, lists, tables and forms get larger row height and padding plus rounder section corners automatically. Section headers use title case, no longer forced to all caps. Use Form .grouped to pick up the layout metrics.
listRowSeparator is only a preference; the list style decides in the end. listRowInsets overrides default row padding. Apple gives no further advice on when to override either.
Use NavigationSplitView and inspector(isPresented:) for sidebar/inspector layouts; remove custom backgrounds on split views and toolbars; trailing inspector state is restored by the framework.

presentationSizing: on macOS .automatic resolves to .form.fitted(horizontal: false, vertical: true). .form suits forms; .page is roughly a sheet of paper for informational content; .fitted uses the content's ideal size and is user-resizable on macOS unless given a fixed frame.

HIG macOS sheets: a modal card over a dimmed parent; give it a reasonable default size (resizing optional); one sheet at a time; use a panel for repeated input. Sheets and popovers adopt Liquid Glass, so remove custom background views.

ContentUnavailableView is the recommended view when content can't be shown (empty list, no search results, network error); there is a built-in .search variant. HIG: empty states should give a next step, ideally with a button.

GroupBox draws a stylized box with an optional label. HIG Boxes: a border or background color by default; on macOS the title sits above; keep boxes small; don't nest boxes; use a sentence-case title. Apple never calls it a 'card'.
badge(_:) shows short supplementary info and appears in list rows, tab bars, toolbar items and menus. No macOS-specific limits are stated.

Liquid Glass is the functional layer for controls and navigation. Don't use it in the content layer (except transient states of sliders and toggles), and use it sparingly on custom controls. Use standard materials for content-layer backgrounds. Use clear glass only over rich media.
glassEffect(_:in:) defaults to the regular glass in a capsule. Combine several effects in a GlassEffectContainer for performance and morphing, and limit how many effects are on screen.
.glass and .glassProminent (the latter similar to borderedProminent) button styles are available. Prefer them to hand-built glass effects. Avoid crowding or layering glass on glass.

Standard bars (toolbars), sheets, popovers, menus, controls and sidebars adopt Liquid Glass automatically. Apple says to remove custom backgrounds or visual-effect views from toolbars, split views, sheets and popovers.

Menu icons (HIG updated June 2026): use them sparingly and with purpose (common actions, key features, locations, devices, visual concepts, user content); omit an icon if none fits; icons for all items in a group or none; use the standard system icons for Copy, Share, Delete etc.

Menus adopt Liquid Glass and menu items for common actions show icons; the system assigns icons to standard actions (Cut/Copy/Paste) based on their standard selectors (AppKit/UIKit mechanism; the SwiftUI equivalent is not stated).

Group logically related items and separate groups with a separator; keep all related commands in one group even when some are used rarely; put important items first; use one level of submenus, not indentation. Context menus: about three groups at most.

Alerts and dialogs: the default button goes on the trailing side of a row (top of a stack), Cancel usually on the leading side. Never make Cancel the default. If people should read before acting, make no button the default.

Destructive context-menu items go last and are marked destructive (red); the HIG states this for iOS, iPadOS and visionOS, and its macOS position is not stated. SwiftUI shows a destructive button in a context menu with a red foreground.
Title-style capitalization for menu items, menu bar titles, button labels (verb first), table column headings and list/form section headers.

Exceptions: alert titles use sentence case if they are a full sentence, title case if a fragment; the Alerts page says alert button titles use sentence case, which conflicts with the Buttons page; box titles use sentence case. Window title case is not stated (keep titles under 15 characters, never the app name).

Append the ellipsis character (…) to a menu item that needs more input before completing, and to a macOS push button that opens another window, view or app. Menu bar examples: Settings…, Open…, Rename…, Export As…, Print….

Use role: .destructive for deleting data or irreversible operations; the system tints it red. Never give the primary/default role to a destructive button. In alerts, use the destructive style only for an action the person didn't deliberately choose (not for 'Empty Trash' after choosing Empty Trash), and always include Cancel.
Don't show an alert for common, undoable destructive actions; reserve confirmation for uncommon actions that can't be undone. Use the caution symbol sparingly on macOS.

Keep prominent buttons to one or two per view, using style rather than size to mark the preferred choice. A toolbar has exactly one prominent primary action, on the trailing side. Color only one control's glass background.

Context menus: keep them short and relevant; every item must also exist in the main UI (on macOS the menu bar lists all commands); don't show keyboard shortcuts in them; hide unavailable items (macOS exception: Cut/Copy/Paste may dim); one submenu level; support them consistently.

Use system (dynamic) colors, never hard-coded values or repurposed semantics. The user's macOS accent color replaces the app accent unless set to multicolor (fixed-color sidebar icons are exempt). The primary role uses accent, destructive uses system red. Never use color alone to convey information. Give custom colors light, dark and increased-contrast variants.

The HIG gives no macOS spacing or margin numbers (only tvOS and visionOS); it says to respect system safe areas, margins and layout guides, and Adopting Liquid Glass says to use standard spacing and not hard-code control layout metrics. Specific numbers given: 44x44 pt minimum hit region; about 10 px inside image buttons.
.padding() with no length uses a platform- and context-appropriate default amount (the number is not stated). On macOS, scenePadding gives the recommended spacing around a window's root view.
Make custom shapes concentric with their containers (ConcentricRectangle, rect(corners:isUniform:)); standard toolbar components already have concentric corner radii.

To separate controls from content, use the scroll edge effect (automatic for system bars; safeAreaBar for custom bars), not a solid or semi-opaque background under controls. Use backgroundExtensionEffect to extend content under a sidebar or inspector.

Every app command belongs in the menu bar (standard menu order, Show/Hide Sidebar in View, a Window menu even with one window), with standard shortcuts kept; disable unavailable items rather than hiding them.

Hide a toolbar item with ToolbarContent.hidden(_:), not by hiding its view (which leaves an empty glass item). Give every icon-only item an accessibility label. Don't mix text and icons on one shared background.
macOS: avoid critical controls or information at the bottom of a window or sidebar, because people often push the bottom edge off screen.
